pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Why Earthquakes Happen — rocks underground are pushed until they suddenly move or break along a fault, releasing energy that travels out as shaking; the underground CAUSE is distinct from the surface EFFECT.

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement):** In England, earthquakes are taught in KS2 **Geography** (physical geography: volcanoes and earthquakes), not KS2 science. The underlying mechanism (plate tectonics, forces in rock) is DfE **KS3** (Geography, and science 'structure of the Earth'). So this causal model runs ahead of the KS2 science sequence — frame via Geography.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No elementary PE names earthquake mechanism directly; earthquakes appear as a mapped feature in **4-ESS2-2** ('patterns of Earth's features'; clarification includes earthquakes) and as a rapid Earth event in **2-ESS1-1**. The stress-release/plate-boundary mechanism is developed at **MS-ESS2-2/3**. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Builds on 'What Is an Earthquake' (5–7, shaking can be strong/weak). The one new idea is CAUSE: stuck rocks under growing push suddenly slip or snap, and the released energy is what shakes the ground. Keep it pre-plate-tectonics (rocks move/break underground); the plate-boundary explanation is the next topic. Separate cause (underground) from effect (surface shaking, felt damage).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A/B boundary (concrete cause→effect, early mechanism). Children can grasp 'stuck then suddenly slips → shaking' with a physical model but tend to picture the ground simply 'opening up'. Success = state that earthquakes are caused by rock suddenly moving/breaking underground and that the shaking is released energy spreading out from that spot.
bestPractices: Make the cause a build-then-release story: push slowly, resistance grows, then a SUDDEN slip — the suddenness is why shaking is violent even though plates creep slowly.
Use a hands-on stick-slip analogy (push two rough blocks/bricks past each other until they jerk; snap a dry stick/spaghetti) so the release is felt, then map it to rock underground.
Explicitly separate the underground cause from the surface effect: draw the slip at depth (the focus) and the shaking spreading up and out to where people feel it.
Correct the 'ground opens and swallows people' image directly and reassuringly — the ground shakes and can crack, but the main hazard is shaking, and most earthquakes are small.
Introduce 'energy travels out as shaking (waves)' informally as ripples spreading from the slip point, seeding the later idea of seismic waves without formal wave vocabulary.
keyRepresentations: Two rough blocks pushed until they suddenly jerk (stick-slip friction model) — the canonical analogy for fault movement
Snapping a bent stick or dry spaghetti to model slow bending then sudden break + release
Cross-section showing the underground slip (focus) with shaking rippling up to the surface
Ripples spreading on water / a shaken tabletop as an image of energy travelling outward from one spot
commonMisconceptions: Earthquakes happen because the ground simply 'opens up' and swallows things (the cause is rock slipping/breaking; large open chasms are rare).
The shaking starts everywhere at once (energy spreads OUT from the slip point, arriving and fading with distance).
Rocks move smoothly and slowly, so shaking should be gentle (rocks stick then release suddenly — the sudden slip causes strong shaking).
Earthquakes are caused by the weather, or by volcanoes only (most are caused by rock movement underground along faults).
The cause and the shaking are the same thing (the underground slip is the cause; the felt shaking is its effect).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach that earthquakes are caused by rocks underground being pushed until they suddenly slip or break along a crack (a fault), releasing energy that spreads outward as shaking. The central insight is the slow build-up then SUDDEN release, and the separation of the underground CAUSE from the surface EFFECT (felt shaking and cracks). Keep it pre-plate-tectonics: rocks move/break underground. A hands-on or simulated stick-slip model makes the build-then-snap tangible; a labelled cross-section supports the cause/effect distinction; targeted questioning and myth-busting address the 'ground swallows people' and 'earthquake weather' ideas.

activities.title: Feel the stick-then-slip: a build-up-then-release model
feedback: If the child predicts a steady, smooth glide, draw attention to what actually happened: it stayed stuck, then jerked. Ask what had to build up before it moved.
If they say the band or rock 'just moves', point to the moment of delay-then-jolt and name it: stuck (stress building), then sudden slip.

Reinforce: the suddenness of the slip is why the ground shakes, and in big earthquakes the shaking can be strong, even though the push was slow — real rock faults can build up strain slowly then release all at once.
activities.rationale: A build-then-release model lets children feel the delay-then-jolt — a time sequence that a still picture cannot show — seeding the mechanism that stuck rock slips suddenly. Predicting before pulling surfaces whether a child assumes motion is always smooth.
sourceClaims: Earthquakes are caused by a sudden slip of rock along a fault (elastic rebound / stick-slip), releasing energy as seismic waves.
learnerActions: Loop an elastic band around a small block or brick sitting on rough sandpaper. Before pulling, PREDICT: as the far end of the band is pulled slowly and steadily, will the block slide smoothly and evenly, or do something else — and WHY?

Pull the band slowly and watch: usually the block stays STUCK while the band stretches (tension builds), then suddenly JERKS forward — stick, then slip. Repeat several times and notice whether it happens the same way each time.
As an alternative release model, slowly bend a dry stick or piece of dry spaghetti and feel the slow bend end in a sudden snap.
Map the model to the ground: the stuck block is like rocks underground being pushed; the sudden jerk is the slip that causes an earthquake.

Optionally work a simulated side-view fault rig: slowly crank a push on two rough rock blocks, watch a stress meter climb while the blocks stay stuck, then see them snap and ripples race up to houses that wobble harder near the slip and gently far away; reset and repeat.
activities.intendedInsight: Force can build up while nothing visibly moves, then release all at once; this sudden slip of underground rock is why the ground shakes, sometimes strongly, even though the pushing is slow and invisible.

activities.title: Cross-section: where the cause is and how shaking spreads
feedback: If a child treats the surface shaking as the cause, point back to the slip point at depth and ask what happened there first.
If they think shaking starts everywhere at once, trace the arrows outward from the slip point and note it arrives and fades with distance.
Confirm when they can point to the underground slip as cause and the surface shaking as effect.
activities.rationale: A labelled cross-section makes the spatial separation of underground cause and surface effect explicit and gives a place to represent energy spreading outward. It supports the distinction but cannot by itself deliver the build-then-snap dynamic, so pair it with a release model.
learnerActions: Study (or draw) a side-view cutaway of the ground showing two rough rock blocks meeting along a fault line, the slip point deep underground, and arrows of shaking rising up to houses on the surface.
Tap or point to reveal/label: the fault, the underground slip point (the cause), and the shaking spreading up and outward to the surface (the effect).
Mark where the shaking would be strongest (near the slip) and where it would be gentler (far away).
Say in your own words which part is the CAUSE (underground slip) and which is the EFFECT (surface shaking and cracks).
activities.intendedInsight: The underground slip is the cause; the felt surface shaking is its effect, and the energy spreads out from one spot rather than starting everywhere at once.

activities.title: Myth-buster: does the ground swallow people?
feedback: If the child says the ground opening is what causes the shaking, clarify that rocks slipping past each other cause it; cracking is a possible effect, not the cause.
If they blame hot or still weather, confront it directly and reassuringly: no weather causes earthquakes; they come from underground rock movement.
Reassure that most earthquakes are small and the main danger is shaking, correcting frightening cartoon images.
activities.rationale: These are named, common misconceptions at this age; addressing them directly and reassuringly separates cause from effect and removes a frightening but inaccurate image.
sourceClaims: The common fear that the ground opens and swallows people is a misconception; ground shaking is the primary hazard.
learnerActions: Consider the question 'Does the ground open up and swallow people in an earthquake?' and predict the answer.
Reveal/discuss the answer: no — the ground shakes and can crack, but the main hazard is the shaking; huge open chasms are rare, and most earthquakes are small.
Discuss a second myth: 'Can a hot, still, sunny day cause an earthquake?' Explain why not — earthquakes come from rock moving underground, not from weather.
State what actually causes an earthquake in your own words, rejecting the 'ground opens up' and 'earthquake weather' explanations.
activities.intendedInsight: Earthquakes are caused by rock slipping/breaking underground along faults, not by the ground opening to swallow things and not by the weather; shaking (not swallowing) is the primary hazard.

activities.title: Explain and check the cause→effect chain
feedback: Gap response (blames weather or says 'the ground just shakes'): reteach with the stick-slip model — stress builds on a fault, snaps, energy travels up; cause below, effect above.
Partial response (knows something underground moves but can't separate cause from effect, or mixes in opening/weather ideas): ask specifically WHERE the cause is and WHAT travels to the surface.
Full response: confirm they distinguished the underground cause from the surface shaking and described energy spreading outward.
activities.rationale: Asking WHERE and WHAT caused the shaking discriminates 'something underground suddenly moved' from surface-only or weather explanations, requiring the child to construct the causal chain — the stick-slip mechanism — rather than only recognise it.
sourceClaims: Earthquakes are caused by a sudden slip of rock along a fault (elastic rebound / stick-slip), releasing energy as seismic waves.
learnerActions: Answer: 'When you feel an earthquake, the ground at the surface shakes. But what actually happened to CAUSE it, and where — at the surface, or somewhere else?'
Put the stages in order: rocks pushed → stuck → sudden slip → shaking spreads to the surface.

Answer probing questions: Is the cause at the surface where we stand, or deeper down? What travels through the ground from the underground movement to make things shake? How does the underground slip reach us up at the surface?

Give a full explanation that rocks underground suddenly move/break along a fault, releasing energy that travels as waves to shake the surface, clearly naming the underground cause and the surface effect.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can state that earthquakes are caused by rock suddenly moving/breaking underground and that the shaking is released energy spreading out from that spot to the surface.

constraints: Keep this pre-plate-tectonics: describe rocks moving/breaking underground along a fault, not plate boundaries — the plate-boundary explanation is the next topic.
Builds on prior understanding that shaking can be strong or weak; the one new idea here is the CAUSE (stuck rocks under growing push suddenly slip or snap, releasing energy that shakes the ground).
Introduce 'energy travels out as shaking (waves)' informally — ripples spreading from the slip point — without formal seismic-wave vocabulary.
Keep the surface cracking/damage framed as an effect, and address the swallowing image reassuringly; most earthquakes are small.

A multiple-choice or sequencing check (e.g. 'What actually causes an earthquake?' with a 'ground opens up' distractor) can confirm the cause→effect chain but only verifies recognition; it does not by itself elicit the child independently constructing or feeling the mechanism.
A static cross-section supports the cause/effect distinction but cannot show the build-then-snap time sequence; pair it with a physical or simulated release model.

Standards placement: in England earthquakes sit in KS2 Geography (physical geography), with the mechanism a later KS3 topic; in NGSS the mechanism is developed at middle school, so this causal model runs ahead of elementary science — frame accordingly.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two USGS-attributed claims (stick-slip/elastic rebound causing seismic waves; the swallowing myth) are marked verified:false in the source row; treat them as unverified pending review. They are cited as sourceClaims only where they directly describe the mechanism being taught or assessed, but their verification status is unconfirmed.

The NGSS 4-ESS2-2 claim supports only standards placement (topic), not the cross-section teaching principle, so learn.activities[1].sourceClaims is [] rather than citing it — independently re-verified in this review.

The legacy entry asserted 'no static image can convey' the concept and '3D adds cost without new insight'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by catalog ratings; softened here to narrow affordance/limit statements (a still picture cannot show a time sequence; 3D is an optional extension), not universal medium-superiority claims.
A simulated 'stress meter' and buildings wobbling by distance are retained as optional feedback examples illustrating the mechanism, not as mandatory or tested mechanisms.

assess.poeTask: Loop an elastic band around a small block or brick sitting on rough sandpaper. Ask the child to PREDICT what the block will do as you slowly and steadily pull the far end of the band — will it slide smoothly and evenly, or something else, and WHY? A child who assumes motion is smooth predicts a steady glide; what actually happens is the block STAYS STUCK while the band stretches (stress builds), then suddenly JERKS forward — stick, then slip. Pull it to check. The prediction and reason given before pulling reveal whether they grasp that force can build up while nothing moves and then release suddenly — exactly how stress builds on a fault and releases as an earthquake.
probeDeeper: The rocks underground were stuck, then suddenly slipped. How does that reach us up at the surface?
Is the CAUSE of the earthquake at the surface where we stand, or deeper down?
Could a hot sunny day cause an earthquake? Why or why not?
What travels through the ground from the underground movement to make things shake?
assess.correctAnswer: The shaking is caused by rocks deep UNDERGROUND suddenly moving or breaking along a crack (a fault). That sudden movement releases energy that travels outward as waves and shakes the ground at the surface. So the cause is underground; the shaking we feel is the surface effect.

errorPatterns.pattern: Earthquakes are caused by the weather ('earthquake weather' — hot, still days)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront it — earthquakes come from rock movement underground, not weather; no weather causes them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes the quake to weather, temperature, or the air.

errorPatterns.pattern: The shaking just happens at the surface — nothing underground (no cause/effect separation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a stick-slip model — stress builds on a fault, snaps, waves travel up; cause below, effect above.
errorPatterns.distractor: The ground just shakes on its own at the surface.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes only surface shaking; can't point to an underground cause.

errorPatterns.pattern: The ground shakes because it opens up / cracks apart (confuses cause with the swallowing myth)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rocks slipping past each other cause it; the ground doesn't open to swallow people.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the ground opening is what causes the shaking.

responseLevels.gap: Attributes earthquakes to weather or 'the ground just shaking'; no underground cause.
responseLevels.full: Explains rocks underground suddenly move/break along a fault, releasing energy that travels as waves to shake the surface — clearly distinguishing the underground cause from the surface effect.
responseLevels.partial: Knows something underground moves but can't clearly separate the underground cause from the surface shaking, or mixes in the opening/weather ideas.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: When you feel an earthquake, the ground at the surface shakes. But what actually happened to CAUSE it, and where did that happen — at the surface, or somewhere else?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can say 'the ground shakes' (the effect) without knowing the underground cause, or blame the weather. Asking WHERE and WHAT caused it separates 'something underground suddenly moved' from surface-only or weather explanations.

sources.claim: Earthquakes are a mapped Earth feature at the elementary level in NGSS 4-ESS2-2 (clarification includes earthquakes); the tectonic mechanism is developed at middle school.
In England earthquakes are taught in KS2 Geography (physical geography), not KS2 science; the mechanism is a later (KS3) topic.
